\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-7x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Find the general solution to the system of ODEs above.

*Hint: ![](images/4c/4c7ca8aa3fb83e7c4ce806080257e8f3b3d5186e19f10649a0bed7202f6501b6.svg) where ![](images/04/0492dd33f8d39d4a74139be25415d6d943888d8ccbf67158690f0960c5334415.svg)*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/85/85304407fca2ace2d7fb5d97123e1f27f45386c8f3ebcc1a1c3859d1b573d2b0.svg)
where ![](images/81/81bcc770826e2156f310569f014356cc686541259c11aa190ac28394a6d38725.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/31/310669815cad029379ffa4022fa9094ef8597d91496c57f70c66ed51926836b3.svg)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by
![](images/e1/e128d7d4610a3a9021b1391f278822bcdf113570500b822c05370e473923f5b7.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-7t} & t{e}^{-7t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-7t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-7t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{-7t} \\ {e}^{-7t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7t},\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229143 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5d3d32e6-9123-5862-a54d-5cd0459cabee" "question-32d4b06d-f6f3-5351-bf77-6d5871dae39c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186228918 :question/problem "![](images/6e/6e456b14ca5110a5cf290cd0053bd52652c8d44e2e9f517f73d2b257c355b8cf.svg)
Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ![](images/e4/e43485cd9eaca81dd04089924a83a909594e575d76d195850cf11719809acbbd.svg) where ![](images/6a/6ac1e35cee6cfbab9771278c3a68f422e5422ef79e4f516755e35748ea402e08.svg)*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/b4/b434d5c8a601c3d7fae734a5b78437457fab7877fe0ca1ff466197817d9d1c0e.svg)
where ![](images/cc/cc9313ae17390c751e51673c53d788c24308f501fa7107e3098cd370028eb1d2.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/1d/1d3df45727a13bfbc41ab2689fd1a9a6dbcc28fd4ed071a430a2e745e99aeec8.svg)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{x}(0),
$$

where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{x}(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by

![](images/a9/a998751dcfc2e8acb4e142c5b4a5241ec61fe3bc087dccf9fe87344d73b04ce3.svg)

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229144 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e674cbe1-254a-5d93-a9b4-be22a2029aaf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186228917 :question/problem "![](images/b0/b0d7ecb854b93b475f1897f7ae66e0e459a5ad22247a9d9a5c11adff32b747e4.svg)
Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ![](images/50/50c3d207258cc321a19532b7b54da568a4a6361dde55f35247fe60e931fe5f93.svg) where ![](images/59/599d579a41d84635ae3a34867759b69af6b406d433c4c11a53898f69e856371e.svg)*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/6d/6dfab7c1edb51450a9238b3fd1154c7d4a5dccb47c689c54768c4b6cc952c068.svg)
where ![](images/eb/eb99201c10627a06594c4967ac8f3a56cb75784f1f824332a9b58a10aaf672bc.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/e7/e70ec908edd1985f4f1f719dceee192536c0bcdf0b4deedcf1c9f785005ee041.svg)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \mathbf{c} =e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t = t_0,$ we have 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c},
$$

and since $e^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
\mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $\mathbf{x}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229145 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7ee364d4-3865-58d1-b13b-994e56af1ccf" "question-c3c2f127-8fe3-52c5-8ea9-fa818612f56c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186228911 :question/problem "Consider the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
\Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \qquad \Phi_0(0) = I_n.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ passing through $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ is presented below. 

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}$  

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,\mathbf{c}$ for some constant vector $\mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At}\,\mathbf{c}$ 

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t_0)=e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $(e^{A t_0})^{-1} \mathbf{x}(t_0)=(e^{At_0})^{-1} e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{c} = e^{-A t_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} e^{-At_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L8}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At - At_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L9}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{A(t-t_0)} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

Fill in the blanks to justify each step of the following reasoning.

$\qquad$ Line $\textrm{L5}$ follows from $\textrm{L4}$ by ![](images/b2/b2df506469d945a843b7784f38a1b12d6f89016aee1fb12581705b6d9d98baab.svg)

$\qquad$ The property of the matrix exponential used in $\textrm{L8}$ is ![](images/7a/7af985a90d901c63f7d03feda679d513fa18ccb36d34c8fb237ac755baf9f801.svg)

$\qquad$ Line $\textrm{L9}$ follows from $\textrm{L8}$ by the fact that  ![](images/c5/c55c24e30a71bf93cdd21c2a5d0f3c68271cd6fb3f2033b84ce8338569eacd4a.svg)" :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\textrm{L4}$ and $\textrm{L5}.$ Starting from $\textrm{L4},$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0)=e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c},
$$

we multiply both sides on the left by $(e^{At_0})^{-1}$ to get

$$
(e^{A t_0})^{-1}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=(e^{At_0})^{-1}e^{A t_0}\,\mathbf{c},
$$

which is line $\textrm{L5}.$ Therefore, $\textrm{L5}$ follows from $\textrm{L4}$ by ![](images/22/2226897d3c49c80358dc93ec1d1d80bd8b513764e6b39bbf93408215c83144bf.svg)

- Next, we justify the step $\textrm{L7}$ to $\textrm{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-At_0$ commute, we may combine exponentials:

$$
e^{At}e^{-At_0}=e^{At-At_0}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\textrm{L7}$ produces line $\textrm{L8}.$ Hence, the property of the matrix exponential used in $\textrm{L8}$ is ![](images/e4/e4a1c6f6b74ea7491973a3bfa76225f1f6af67a681582a49afa51772c05bfaed.svg)

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L8}$ and $\textrm{L9}.$ Starting from $\textrm{L8},$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At-At_0}\mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

we rewrite the exponent using the algebraic identity $At-At_0=A(t-t_0)$ to get

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

which is line $\textrm{L9}.$ Thus, $\textrm{L9}$ follows from $\textrm{L8}$ by the fact that $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{At-At_0=A(t-t_0)\text{ for any }t\text{ and }t_0}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-964cfe5a-540f-5a2a-90eb-038dd13a228b" :question/id #uuid "964cfe5a-540f-5a2a-90eb-038dd13a228b" :question/math-academy-id "q-334778" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d08bec31-d229-5948-b097-4d0df5e00ec6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$*" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0f0167e8-c854-5755-b6be-76017465421b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

$$

$$

:db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186230188 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/f9/f94140f8c9fe736ca7c574547658856e85d938eb08064046716be8eb1a2748de.svg)
where ![](images/26/26dcf2c367c915460d09f4f38b40e4f792a06b6ab44291b4739a6935529daf89.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/90/9000e03ddf617a1e3c4e0eed5da2b846d62e3d68588b601d90643783960d17df.svg)

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
![](images/11/11e0da79656b7f8e2c84c6c54e6dd6b54cf53cbb8e746d44dfb13329c3d2ed8f.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

1\. *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

  $$
  e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
  $$

2\. *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

  $$
  (e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
  $$

3\. *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

  $$
  e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
  $$

4\. *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

  $$
  e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
  $$

  **Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

Let's see how these properties can be used in practice." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229256 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

"c3c2f127-8fe3-52c5-8ea9-fa818612f56c" :question/math-academy-id "q-337108" :question/problem "Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L8}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2},$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Using $\text{L1}$, we substitute ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ into this equation to obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

which is line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}\text{ into }x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L7}.$ Using line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

From line $\text{L6}$, we know that $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}).$ Substituting this expression for $c$ into the formula for $x(t)$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L8}$ and $\text{L9}.$ Starting from $\text{L8},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

we rewrite the exponent using the algebraic identity $At-A{t}_{0}=A(t-{t}_{0})$ to get

$$
x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L9}.$ Thus, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L8}$ by the fact that $At-A{t}_{0}=A(t-{t}_{0})\text{ for any }t\text{ and }{t}_{0}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186230188 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/f9/f94140f8c9fe736ca7c574547658856e85d938eb08064046716be8eb1a2748de.svg)
where ![](images/26/26dcf2c367c915460d09f4f38b40e4f792a06b6ab44291b4739a6935529daf89.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/90/9000e03ddf617a1e3c4e0eed5da2b846d62e3d68588b601d90643783960d17df.svg)

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get
![](images/11/11e0da79656b7f8e2c84c6c54e6dd6b54cf53cbb8e746d44dfb13329c3d2ed8f.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

Let's see more examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186230193 :tutorial/content "Now, let's find the solution to the initial value problem below

Recall that the general solution of the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Evaluating both sides of $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \mathbf{c}$ at $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & ={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c \\ x(0) & ={e}^{A(0)}\,c \\ x(0) & =I\,c \\ c & =x(0).\end{aligned}

Thus, the solution to our initial value problem is 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{x}(0).
$$

Computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{7t} & t{e}^{7t} \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(3-2t){e}^{7t} \\ -2{e}^{7t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}.$ We can determine the constant vector $\mathbf{c}$ using the initial condition at time $t=t_0{:}$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c} \implies \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

since the inverse of $e^{At_0}$ is $e^{-At_0}.$ Plugging this back into our general solution gives the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our specific problem (with $t_0=1$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

1\. *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

  $$
  e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
  $$

2\. *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

  $$
  (e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
  $$

3\. *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

  $$
  e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
  $$

4\. *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

  $$
  e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
  $$

  **Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

Let's see how these properties can be used in practice." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186229256 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186228910 :question/problem "$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].$*"] ["question-232a3dab-08a5-5200-8a90-246a69a099b3" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$

</tbody></table>"] ["question-e674cbe1-254a-5d93-a9b4-be22a2029aaf" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-3)}\,x(3) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-3)} & (t-3){e}^{4(t-3)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-3)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,-{e}^{4(t-3)}\, \\ \,0\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e674cbe1-254a-5d93-a9b4-be22a2029aaf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c45903a1-fe5a-5b4c-96af-6a0c00ecf707" :answer-field/id #uuid You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the definition of ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ as the standard fundamental matrix by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by  
{{field-3}}."] ["question-7ee364d4-3865-58d1-b13b-994e56af1ccf" :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t=0$ to obtain

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is line $\text{L3}.$ Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L4}.$ By definition, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ satisfies the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

The second condition here is exactly line $\text{L4},$ so $\text{L4}$ follows from the definition of ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ as the standard fundamental matrix by $\text{using the initial condition }{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we have ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Substituting ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$ into $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L5}.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{substituting }{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}\text{ into }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$"] ["question-c3c2f127-8fe3-52c5-8ea9-fa818612f56c" :question/math-academy-id "q-337108"] ["question-c3c2f127-8fe3-52c5-8ea9-fa818612f56c" :question/problem "Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L8}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}."] ["question-c3c2f127-8fe3-52c5-8ea9-fa818612f56c" :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2},$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Using $\text{L1}$, we substitute ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ into this equation to obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

which is line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}\text{ into }x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L7}.$ Using line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

From line $\text{L6}$, we know that $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}).$ Substituting this expression for $c$ into the formula for $x(t)$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L8}$ and $\text{L9}.$ Starting from $\text{L8},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

we rewrite the exponent using the algebraic identity $At-A{t}_{0}=A(t-{t}_{0})$ to get

$$
x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L9}.$ Thus, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L8}$ by the fact that $At-A{t}_{0}=A(t-{t}_{0})\text{ for any }t\text{ and }{t}_{0}.$"] "question-c3c2f127-8fe3-52c5-8ea9-fa818612f56c"] [17592186230188 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](images/f9/f94140f8c9fe736ca7c574547658856e85d938eb08064046716be8eb1a2748de.svg)
where ![](images/26/26dcf2c367c915460d09f4f38b40e4f792a06b6ab44291b4739a6935529daf89.svg) So, the matrix of the system is ![](images/90/9000e03ddf617a1e3c4e0eed5da2b846d62e3d68588b601d90643783960d17df.svg)

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

$$

$$

$$

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \qquad \Phi_0(0) = I_n.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ passing through $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ is presented below. 

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}$  

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,\mathbf{c}$ for some constant vector $\mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At}\,\mathbf{c}$ 

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t_0)=e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $(e^{A t_0})^{-1} \mathbf{x}(t_0)=(e^{At_0})^{-1} e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{c} = e^{-A t_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} e^{-At_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L8}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At - At_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L9}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{A(t-t_0)} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

Fill in the blanks to justify each step of the following reasoning.

- We first consider lines $\textrm{L4}$ and $\textrm{L5}.$ Starting from $\textrm{L4},$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0)=e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c},
$$

we multiply both sides on the left by $(e^{At_0})^{-1}$ to get

$$
(e^{A t_0})^{-1}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=(e^{At_0})^{-1}e^{A t_0}\,\mathbf{c},
$$

$$
e^{At}e^{-At_0}=e^{At-At_0}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\textrm{L7}$ produces line $\textrm{L8}.$ Hence, the property of the matrix exponential used in $\textrm{L8}$ is ![](images/ba/bab6ad7c1621beb36d016e72f1e040206b9bf70a2e21ff266ba5b71495a23ae2.png)

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L8}$ and $\textrm{L9}.$ Starting from $\textrm{L8},$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At-At_0}\mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

we rewrite the exponent using the algebraic identity $At-At_0=A(t-t_0)$ to get

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

which is line $\textrm{L9}.$ Thus, $\textrm{L9}$ follows from $\textrm{L8}$ by the fact that $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{At-At_0=A(t-t_0)\text{ for any }t\text{ and }t_0}.$"} {:db/id :question/problem "Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L8}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L7}.$ Using line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

From line $\text{L6}$, we know that $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}).$ Substituting this expression for $c$ into the formula for $x(t)$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L8}$ and $\text{L9}.$ Starting from $\text{L8},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

we rewrite the exponent using the algebraic identity $At-A{t}_{0}=A(t-{t}_{0})$ to get

$$
x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L9}.$ Thus, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L8}$ by the fact that $At-A{t}_{0}=A(t-{t}_{0})\text{ for any }t\text{ and }{t}_{0}.$"} {:db/id 17592186372710 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix.

For example, consider the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=5y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=-5x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ So, the matrix of the system is $[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}]$

Recall that given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Since we have already seen how to compute the standard fundamental matrix, we will not repeat the calculation here. So, computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(5t) & \operatorname{sin}(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}(5t) & \operatorname{cos}(5t)\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(5t) & \operatorname{sin}(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}(5t) & \operatorname{cos}(5t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}(5t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}(5t) \\ \operatorname{cos}(5t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

**Note:** Recall that for the general solution of the ordinary differential equation $x'(t)=ax(t),$ we have 

$$
x'(t)=ax(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
x(t) = c \, e^{at}, 
\quad
c \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Now, for the general solution of the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ we obtain 

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
\quad
\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "978fc2f4-910c-5bef-9ae3-3da9377642ce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14515 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c774d65b-c500-58e4-aa9a-e222d3d136ae" :step/math-academy-id 592270 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230003}} {:db/id 17592186230003 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229142 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228910 :question/id #uuid "26df399d-cd87-5b5d-9f3f-7ced4ca5fd06" :question/math-academy-id "e-21707"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e5bc609b-dc5b-52e9-9f0e-206f32bb829b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050125} {:db/id 17592186050228}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229669} {:db/id 17592186229677} {:db/id 17592186308684} {:db/id 17592186308685} {:db/id 17592186402113}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "d3b52974-38d7-50fa-b648-b51510a9a617" :step/math-academy-id 592271 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230004}} {:db/id 17592186230004 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230193 :tutorial/content "Now, let's find the solution to the initial value problem below

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=7x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=7y(t),\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

where $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ So, the matrix of the system is $[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]$

Recall that the general solution of the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is some constant vector.

Evaluating both sides of $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \mathbf{c}$ at $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & ={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c \\ x(0) & ={e}^{A(0)}\,c \\ x(0) & =I\,c \\ c & =x(0).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to our initial value problem is 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{x}(0).
$$

Computing the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}{e}^{7t} & t{e}^{7t} \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{7t} & t{e}^{7t} \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(3-2t){e}^{7t} \\ -2{e}^{7t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9cb11887-9535-5a54-a180-eb20a7534696" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14529 :tutorial/title "Solving Initial Value Problems"} :step/id #uuid "5206e604-fe74-5b8a-800c-cdb747dc1e28" :step/math-academy-id 592274 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230005}} {:db/id 17592186230005 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229143 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228918 :question/id #uuid "ead811e0-8551-5b15-8b49-711cbe0b8498" :question/math-academy-id "e-21725"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d611c75-818f-508f-a7a4-49edb32baa41" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229657} {:db/id 17592186229682} {:db/id 17592186308537} {:db/id 17592186311559} {:db/id 17592186311560} {:db/id 17592186311561} {:db/id 17592186311562} {:db/id 17592186311563} {:db/id 17592186372698} {:db/id 17592186372703}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential"} :step/id #uuid "c93fbf09-3c42-5a66-8e76-1cf0d810f44a" :step/math-academy-id 592275 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230006}} {:db/id 17592186230006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230194 :tutorial/content "Next, let's find the solution to the initial value problem 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=-7y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=7x(t),\end{aligned}
$$

given that $[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(7t) & -\operatorname{sin}(7t) \\ \operatorname{sin}(7t) & \operatorname{cos}(7t)\end{aligned}]$ where $[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ So, the matrix of the system is $[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}.$ We can determine the constant vector $\mathbf{c}$ using the initial condition at time $t=t_0{:}$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c} \implies \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

since the inverse of $e^{At_0}$ is $e^{-At_0}.$ Plugging this back into our general solution gives the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our specific problem (with $t_0=1$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(7(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sin}(7(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sin}(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}(7(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}(7(t-1)) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}(7(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0fe9a975-9d92-5f79-8a67-34af55196fb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14530 :tutorial/title "Solving Initial Value Problems With Shifted Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "19b34f7c-755c-5e1b-a16f-22bd17d1ecc7" :step/math-academy-id 592278 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230007}} {:db/id 17592186230007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229144 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228917 :question/id #uuid "b061f2b1-b015-582f-921f-9b444db631ee" :question/math-academy-id "e-21723"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37e58bb6-6d90-5171-bba2-6ffa5a0c91d9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229664} {:db/id 17592186229684} {:db/id 17592186311564} {:db/id 17592186311590} {:db/id 17592186311591} {:db/id 17592186311592} {:db/id 17592186311593} {:db/id 17592186311594} {:db/id 17592186391579} {:db/id 17592186391586}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "633a401e-5116-5c9e-a0b4-8848cf596d7b" :step/math-academy-id 592279 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230008}} {:db/id 17592186230008 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

- *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

$$
e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
$$

- *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

$$
(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
$$

- *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

$$
e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
$$

- *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

$$
e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
$$

**Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

Let's see how these properties can be used in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ae3cfa7-a5a5-5a50-aefa-8b8dec561567" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14528 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Properties of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "eb56047e-3845-5f8e-9282-d41f308270e3" :step/math-academy-id 592282 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230009}} {:db/id 17592186230009 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229145 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228911 :question/id #uuid "ace067cd-e1d0-5b3e-bae2-bf58dcac3585" :question/math-academy-id "e-21711"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1ff837c0-0ebb-5a9e-acb4-894261e0318c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186229658} {:db/id 17592186229697} {:db/id 17592186311712} {:db/id 17592186311794} {:db/id 17592186311799} {:db/id 17592186372710} {:db/id 17592186396936} {:db/id 17592186396993}] :knowledge-point/title "Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution: Homogeneous Systems"} :step/id #uuid "6a90e198-ec80-5daf-8cb9-69841a16a32d" :step/math-academy-id 592283}] :activity/title "Solving Homogeneous Systems of ODEs Using Matrix Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186229256} {:db/id 17592186230002 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230188 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving homogeneous systems of the form

{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=-7y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=7x(t),\end{aligned}
$$

given that $[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(7t) & -\operatorname{sin}(7t) \\ \operatorname{sin}(7t) & \operatorname{cos}(7t)\end{aligned}]$ where $[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ So, the matrix of the system is $[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}.$ We can determine the constant vector $\mathbf{c}$ using the initial condition at time $t=t_0{:}$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c} \implies \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

since the inverse of $e^{At_0}$ is $e^{-At_0}.$ Plugging this back into our general solution gives the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our specific problem (with $t_0=1$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(7(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sin}(7(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sin}(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}(7(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}(7(t-1)) \\ -4\operatorname{cos}(7(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0fe9a975-9d92-5f79-8a67-34af55196fb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14530 :tutorial/title "Solving Initial Value Problems With Shifted Conditions"} :step/id #uuid "19b34f7c-755c-5e1b-a16f-22bd17d1ecc7" :step/math-academy-id 592278 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230007}} {:db/id 17592186230194 :tutorial/content "Next, let's find the solution to the initial value problem

- *Law of Exponents:* If $A$ is a constant square matrix, then

$$
e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}\,e^{As}.
$$

- *Inverse:* For any $t,$ the matrix $e^{At}$ is invertible and 

$$
(e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}.
$$

- *Identity:* For any square matrix $A,$

$$
e^{A\cdot 0} = I.
$$

- *Product of exponentials:* If $A$ and $B$ commute (i.e., $AB = BA$), then

$$
e^{A}e^{B} = e^{A+B}.
$$

**Watch out!** In general, this identity is *not true* unless $A$ and $B$ commute.

Let's see how these properties can be used in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ae3cfa7-a5a5-5a50-aefa-8b8dec561567" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14528 :tutorial/title "Reminder: Properties of Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "eb56047e-3845-5f8e-9282-d41f308270e3" :step/math-academy-id 592282 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230009}} {:db/id 17592186230192 :tutorial/content "Before proceeding with the next example, let's recall some important properties of matrix exponentials:

Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in
